svg.title: The CoPP pipeline from the punt path to the CPU, and why a template tuned for steady state breaks at convergence
svg.desc: Top: the pipeline. Packets destined for the device itself leave the forwarding path on the punt path, enter a classifier that sorts them into classes, pass a policer per class, then reach CPU queues and finally the protocol process. CoPP acts at the policer, so it protects the CPU from volume but cannot tell a legitimate flood from an attack - both are dropped. Middle: the four classes that matter with an honest rate and the consequence of tuning them too low. Routing protocol class: needs tens of megabits during a full table update, and at 500 kbps the BGP session resets and re-establishes in a loop. Management class: SSH and SNMP, small but must be guaranteed, or the device becomes unreachable during an incident. Exception class: TTL, ICMP and fragmentation, easy to over-police until PMTUD fails and large packets vanish. Best-effort catch-all: everything else, which should be the only class allowed to drop freely. Bottom: the arithmetic and the two rules. A full BGP table update arrives as tens of megabits of punt traffic against a template rate of 500 kbps, a ratio of two orders of magnitude, and the failure looks like a flapping neighbour rather than a policy. Rule one: measure the punt rate during convergence before choosing the rate. Rule two: keep a lab copy of every CoPP policy, because the failure mode is a device you cannot log into.
svg.text: CoPP protects the CPU from volume, not from intent
The same policer that stops a flood also stops a legitimate full-table update - and both look identical to the classifier.
tens of Mbps during a full update
the neighbour looks flaky; the CoPP policy is the cause, and it is not in the log line anyone reads
you cannot log in during the incident
guarantee it explicitly; a shared best-effort class is how devices become unreachable when busy
the symptom is "the web page loads and the file does not" - nobody blames CoPP
this is the only class that should drop
if this class is generous, the policy protects nothing; if it is tiny, unknown protocols break silently
1 measure the punt rate during convergence before choosing a rate
2 keep a lab copy of every CoPP policy - the failure mode locks you out
Deployment order that avoids the self-inflicted outage: apply the policy with the routing class generous, observe for a week, then tighten. Never the other way round.
If a CoPP change is being made to a device you cannot reach by out-of-band, schedule it with a rollback that a remote hand can execute.
